questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Observed lifetime of a fast particle
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a boosted particle appears to live longer in the laboratory.
questions.stem: Designers of a detector enclosure want to know why a fast particle seems to survive far longer than its rest-frame lifetime.

answer.exemplar: The particle's lifetime is a property of its own rest frame, and that frame is unchanged by the boost; what changes is how much laboratory time elapses while the particle travels. In the laboratory the boosted particle ages more slowly, so its measured lifetime is multiplied by the Lorentz factor. A muon moving at 0.6 of the speed of light therefore lives about 1.25 times longer in the laboratory than the 2.2 microseconds recorded at rest.

questions.explanation: Time dilation means the boosted particle's clock runs slower, so the lab measures a lifetime longer by a factor of gamma. The rest-frame lifetime is unchanged; only the frame of measurement differs.
questions.hint: Multiply the rest lifetime by the Lorentz factor.

questions.topic: Clock error from orbital speed in a navigation system
questions.learningObjective: Explain how orbital speed causes satellite clock drift.
questions.stem: The structural brief explains why a navigation satellite's onboard clock drifts against a ground clock because of its speed.

answer.exemplar: A clock in motion accumulates proper time more slowly than a clock at rest in the observer's frame, so a satellite racing around the Earth at orbital speed keeps slightly less time than a clock on the ground. questions.hint: Rate difference grows with the square of the speed.

answer.exemplar: The relativistic Doppler factor for a source moving straight toward the observer is the square root of one plus beta divided by one minus beta.
